content.raw:
Before the race George Russell called Formula 1's newest circuit "arguably the most risky circuit of the whole calendar, because you have real high-speed corners, sort of Jeddah-esque, and the walls are very close." On Sunday evening Gabriel Bortoleto, asked about the race, said "I almost fell asleep as well." They were describing the same 5.414 kilometres, a few days apart, and they were both right.

The first Grand Prix at the Madring produced four overtakes, by the counts published on Monday. Monaco managed ten this year. The three days before it set an F2 car on fire, put a Haas into the wall hard enough to need a new chassis, and produced a pole position decided by eleven thousandths. None of that is a contradiction. It is what you get when you build a circuit that is very hard to drive and very easy to follow on.

What Madrid built

The circuit runs for 22 corners around the IFEMA exhibition centre on the north-east edge of the city, part public road and part permanent, in the way Miami is. Its signature is La Monumental, a long curve banked at up to 13.5 degrees that the promoters call the longest banked corner in Formula 1. It was designed by Jarno Zaffelli's Studio Dromo. It cost about 83 million euros, of which IFEMA's share is 47.5 million that it does not expect to see back for thirteen years, holds 110,000 people, and has a contract until 2035.

The last time Formula 1 raced in Madrid was 1981, at Jarama, in front of 25,000 people and under threats from ETA. Zaffelli said before the weekend that he hoped people would leave "recognising it's possible to build a street circuit that is not boring." That was the bar he set himself.

What the championship winning car looked like in 1981. Kaiketsu, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Friday and Saturday: the car killer

Formula 2 practice was stopped with Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak's car against the wall at Turn 18 and on fire. He walked away. F2 qualifying was stopped four more times. Arvid Lindblad put his Racing Bulls into the wall at Turn 13 in second practice and the session was red-flagged to recover it. On Saturday morning Alexander Albon tapped a wall early and broke a track rod, Lewis Hamilton locked up at the final corner, slid into the Tecpro and stopped on track with a punctured front tyre, and Oliver Bearman lost the Haas through Turns 10 and 11 and hit the wall hard enough to end the session and his Saturday. Haas said afterwards the damage was too severe to repair before qualifying. Lance Stroll missed qualifying too, with a water pressure problem. Twenty cars set a time.

Carlos Sainz, racing at home, said over the weekend the part nobody in Madrid wanted to hear: that "going at 260km/h, 270km/h on esses that you cannot see through is definitely eye-opening", and that it made him question how safe it all was.

And yet Saturday afternoon was as good a qualifying hour as the season has had. Hamilton held provisional pole after the first runs in Q3. Lando Norris took it off him with a 1:31.824 he called "probably one of the best laps I've done ever in my career", eleven thousandths ahead of Kimi Antonelli, with the top five covered by 0.195s. Charles Leclerc put it plainly afterwards: "It's a great track and honestly I think everybody did a great job with the track as it is, particularly in qualifying."

That is the first half of the verdict. As a place to drive one car as fast as it will go, the Madring works. The drivers were frightened of it in the way they are frightened of Jeddah and Baku, and they respected it for the same reason.

Sunday: the procession

The second half took 57 laps to arrive. Antonelli attacked Norris twice on the opening lap and cut the chicane twice; his explanation in the press conference was the whole race in a sentence: "the second chicane, if I would have turned in, me and Lando would have touched and probably gone in the wall." After that, nothing. Four passes in a season whose races had averaged 61 before this one, a week after Monza had 78.

Esteban Ocon put the mechanical part of it well. The tyres did not degrade and did not grain, so nobody was ever much slower than the car in front, and "if we had a race on Friday, it would have been much better", when the track was still evolving. Lindblad said it "wasn't the most exciting race", which for a rookie is candour. Max Verstappen said what he always says about street circuits, which is that he is not a fan of them.

The specifics were more useful. Bearman on Turn 5, the chicane at the end of the long straight that was supposed to be the overtaking spot: "That kind of curved braking takes away any possibility of different lines and sending one up the inside. So that's a shame and maybe a bit of an oversight." Russell said the Turn 18 and 19 section, which the drivers had taken to calling the roundabout, offered no clear chance. Norris went further: "They should get rid of 18, 19. Useless. Just have more of a straight into a hairpin," with a wide entry like Austin's first corner, because "the fact you have to turn and brake basically defeats the whole object of racing." And then the line that will follow this circuit around: "I don't know how someone looks at this design and goes, mint!"

Albon thought Turn 5 needed the most work, said the drivers had already raised it with the FIA, and hoped for "open-mindedness to make some track changes for next year". His estimate of the job: "I think there only needs to be a couple of changes to fix the problem."

La Monumental, and the cars that drive it

The corner Madrid built the marketing around got the harshest review, and it came from the man with the most laps in Formula 1. Fernando Alonso: "It is sad, you know, in a way, with this generation of cars to come to a very nice circuit like this one, with challenges here and there, like Monumental corner, Turn 12, and the driver input is just nothing." He said his press officer could have driven it. "Michael can drive in Turn 12 because you go flat with no deployment."

That sentence carries the weight of the whole argument. A banked corner is a challenge when a car arrives at it with more speed than grip. Alonso's point is that this generation, with its energy budgets and its active aero, arrives at La Monumental with nothing left to deploy and takes it flat without asking the driver anything. Verstappen's version was that the banking is "cool" but "they should have done it the other way around." The corner was drawn while these cars were largely a set of regulations on paper, and the cars that turned up made it a straight with a view.

The three corners

The fixes were on the table before the race. The Race reported that the organisers had put changes to the FIA ahead of the weekend and deferred them to 2027 because of homologation and a build that only started in April 2025 and lost time to a wet winter. Three areas are marked. The Turn 5 and 6 chicane will be widened and its approach straightened so two cars can arrive side by side. Turn 13, the left-hander after La Monumental, will be tightened into a real braking zone. Turn 20 will be widened, with its entry and barrier line moved, so that a move there is not automatically a crash into Turn 21.

Luis Garcia Abad, the event director, told Motorsport.com: "FIA has clearly defined how to improve the circuit layout, and we will be open to that because we will have to refurbish the circuit for next year." He also said what the promoter is entitled to say: "I really believe that the drivers enjoyed qualifying a lot. But for sure we will try to make an improvement for next year. We have the space, we have a venue, we have the facilities, we have the capacity to do it." Norris wants more than that, the whole of 18 and 19 gone and a straight from 17 into a hairpin at 20. Sainz wants one thing the good street tracks have: "Good street tracks like Baku, Macau tend to have one single overtaking spot with a very long straight. I think we just need to have a look where there's the possibility to add that overtaking spot." Leclerc thinks "just a small change or two small changes could change significantly the racing."

Our view

The drivers had told the FIA which corners would not work, the organisers had put their own list of changes to the FIA before the race, and Sunday did precisely what both predicted. That is the good news, and it is real: nobody is guessing about what to fix, and the circuit has a ten-year contract and a promoter who has already said yes. Widen the chicane, tighten 13, open up 20, and a track with no overtaking spots becomes a track with one or two, which is Baku's number and Jeddah's, and those races are not processions.

What cannot be fixed with concrete is the premise. Every corner on this lap where you might brake alongside another car curves while you are braking, and a circuit that is thrilling alone and hopeless in company is a qualifying circuit with a race attached. The venue did its job, and the drivers who hated the racing liked the place. Madrid has the lap. It has a year to build the race.

Every session is on the Spanish Grand Prix weekend page, qualifying is on the qualifying page and Sunday is on the race page. The Race's account of the changes is here, the FIA's report on Saturday's crashes is here, and RaceFans' first impressions from Friday are here.

Zaffelli wanted people to walk away knowing a street circuit did not have to be boring. On Saturday he had them. On Sunday he lost them, and the FIA already has the list of where.

title.raw: McLaren let him go in November. Madrid made him champion: Ugo Ugochukwu's fifteen-point turnaround
title.rendered: McLaren let him go in November. Madrid made him champion: Ugo Ugochukwu’s fifteen-point turnaround

content.raw:
The Formula 3 championship was decided at about twenty to seven on Friday evening, in a twenty-minute qualifying session that most people at the Madring were not watching. Freddie Slater arrived in Madrid fifteen points clear with three races to go. He qualified seventeenth. Ugo Ugochukwu qualified fourth, and then second in the session that followed, and from that moment the leader was the one chasing.

Two days later Ugochukwu crossed the line second behind Tuukka Taponen to become the first Formula 3 champion from the United States, 159 points to 145. He scored 33 across the weekend. Slater scored four.

Why there were three races

This was not a normal finale. The Bahrain round and its test were cancelled earlier in the year because of the situation in the Middle East, and rather than run a shorter season F3 gave Madrid a second Feature Race on Sunday morning and a second qualifying session to set its grid, which the series described as an additional opportunity to score points after the loss of the Bahrain weekend. Each qualifying session carried two points for pole. The first set the grids for Saturday, with the top twelve reversed for the Sprint; the second set Sunday's.

So the title was settled by a race that was not on the calendar in January, at a circuit that did not exist two years ago, in a format invented for one weekend. Hold that thought, because it matters less than it sounds.

Twenty minutes on Friday

Taito Kato took the first pole of his F3 career in the opening session, a 1:50.535 that beat Pedro Clerot by twelve thousandths, with Tuukka Taponen third and Ugochukwu fourth. Slater, with a car problem, was seventeenth. The second session went to Taponen, at 1:49.750, and Ugochukwu was 0.021s behind him on the front row. Slater recovered to eighth.

Read that as grid slots and the weekend is already written. Ugochukwu would start ninth, fourth and second. Slater would start seventeenth, seventeenth and eighth, at a track where the Formula 1 race two days later produced four overtakes.

Saturday: the lead becomes a tie

The Sprint went to Theophile Nael, who took the lead from James Wharton into the first corner and was never caught, the first race winner at the Madring and his third victory of the season for Campos. Wharton and Alex Powell gave Prema the other two steps of the podium. Ugochukwu was eighth for three points. Slater, from seventeenth, scored nothing. Fifteen became twelve.

The first Feature Race started with a pile-up at Turn 8 that took out roughly a quarter of the field, Bruno del Pino and Enzo Deligny colliding as Van Amersfoort team-mates and collecting five other cars behind them, and a red flag. When it resumed Clerot led every lap from second on the grid for his first win in the category, for Rodin. "We knew it was all about the start, and we nailed it," he said. Kato was second, Taponen third, Ugochukwu fourth for twelve points.

Slater's afternoon went the other way. He touched Hiyu Yamakoshi at the first corner, spent the race in the low teens, locked up into Turn 1 on lap 8 fighting the same car for fourteenth, and on lap 10 spun at Turn 19 and went into the barrier. Out. That left the two of them level on 141 points with one race to run, Ugochukwu ahead on countback because he had more wins, and Campos already the teams' champions for the second year in a row.

Sunday morning: the one-lap shootout

Taponen started Feature Race 2 from pole and held the lead into Turn 1, which made him the first driver all weekend to do so. Ugochukwu followed him through and stayed there. He tried, for a few laps, and then did the arithmetic: "It was quite difficult with the dirty air to overtake Tuukka. I tried my best a few laps, but I saw I couldn't get quite close enough. We knew that P2 would clinch the title, so just had to ultimately bring it home."

Slater, from eighth, dropped to ninth early, took the place back on lap 5, and spent the rest of the race behind Deligny, having a look at Turn 7 on lap 10 and a longer look at Turn 13 on lap 13 without getting either done. With three laps left Yamakoshi's car stopped on the run to Turn 7 and the safety car set up a one-lap restart, which is the kind of thing that ends championships. It did not. Taponen won by 1.398s, his first F3 victory and the first for a Finn, Clerot was third, and Slater finished eighth, exactly where he started.

"Every single kerb felt louder than usual, I started hearing weird sounds," Ugochukwu said afterwards. "Once I crossed the finish line, I could relax. Just really relieved."

The driver McLaren let go

Ugochukwu was born in New York in April 2007 and signed by McLaren's young driver programme in 2021, at thirteen. The junior record is good: Euro 4 champion with Prema in 2023, runner-up in Italian F4 the same year, winner of the Macau Grand Prix in 2024. Then a first F3 season with Prema in 2025 that returned sixteenth in the standings and no wins, and in November McLaren cut him loose along with Martinius Stenshorne and Brando Badoer.

He spent the winter in New Zealand, won the Formula Regional Oceania title with four wins, came back to F3 with Campos, and tested an Alpine at Monza in June. "We were super clinical, no mistakes made the whole weekend," he said on Sunday, "and we just delivered when we had to." That is a fair description of the whole year. Two wins, and a qualifying record that put him in the top four on the only weekend it had to.

And the one who lost it

Slater is eighteen, British, the 2024 Italian F4 champion and the 2025 Formula Regional European champion, and in January Audi made him the first member of its new Driver Development Programme. He drove a rookie F3 season for Trident that most champions would take: eight podiums, a win in Hungary, and the championship lead into the summer break after four Feature Race podiums in a row. Then 15 points in the last five races, and one qualifying session in Madrid that his car did not survive.

He will be in Formula 2 next year with Invicta, announced on Tuesday, two days after losing the title. It is the same Trident-to-Invicta step Gabriel Bortoleto, Leonardo Fornaroli and Rafael Camara took, and all three of them arrived there as F3 champions. Slater arrives as the runner-up who led the most laps of the argument.

Our view

It is tempting to say the extra race decided the championship, and the tempting version is wrong. After Saturday the two were level on points with Ugochukwu ahead on countback. Had Madrid been an ordinary two-race weekend, the title would have gone to the same driver, by tie-break, with an asterisk the size of a season. What Sunday's race did was remove the asterisk. Ugochukwu won it on the road, by fourteen points, having started the decider six places ahead of his rival and finished six places ahead of him.

The weekend also exposed how much of a modern F3 title is qualifying. Slater lost the championship in the twenty minutes on Friday when his car went wrong, not in the wall at Turn 19. At a circuit where nobody passed anybody, seventeenth on the grid was not a place to recover from, and he knew it before the Sprint started.

Where it leaves us

For the books: the first Formula 3 champion from the United States, a fifteen-point deficit turned into a fourteen-point margin in three races, 33 points to 4, a title decided at a circuit that was a building site a year ago in a race that did not exist in January, Campos's second teams' title in a row, first wins for Clerot and Taponen, the first Finnish winner in F3, and the first race of any kind at the Madring going to Theophile Nael.

Every session is on the Madrid weekend page, the final table is on the F3 standings, and the season's results are on the results page. The official reports of Feature Race 1 and Feature Race 2 are on the series site, and Motorsport.com has the fuller interview.

McLaren spent four and a half years developing a Formula 3 champion and let him go a season early. Campos had him for one.

He touched Hiyu Yamakoshi at the first corner, spent the race in the low teens, locked up into Turn 1 on lap 8 fighting the same car for fourteenth, and on lap 10 spun at Turn 19 and went into the barrier. Out. That left the two of them level on 141 points with one race to run, Ugochukwu ahead on countback because he had more wins, and Campos already the teams’ champions for the second year in a row.

Sunday morning: the one-lap shootout

Taponen started Feature Race 2 from pole and held the lead into Turn 1, which made him the first driver all weekend to do so. Ugochukwu followed him through and stayed there. He tried, for a few laps, and then did the arithmetic: “It was quite difficult with the dirty air to overtake Tuukka. I tried my best a few laps, but I saw I couldn’t get quite close enough. We knew that P2 would clinch the title, so just had to ultimately bring it home.”

Slater, from eighth, dropped to ninth early, took the place back on lap 5, and spent the rest of the race behind Deligny, having a look at Turn 7 on lap 10 and a longer look at Turn 13 on lap 13 without getting either done. With three laps left Yamakoshi’s car stopped on the run to Turn 7 and the safety car set up a one-lap restart, which is the kind of thing that ends championships. It did not. Taponen won by 1.398s, his first F3 victory and the first for a Finn, Clerot was third, and Slater finished eighth, exactly where he started.

“Every single kerb felt louder than usual, I started hearing weird sounds,” Ugochukwu said afterwards. “Once I crossed the finish line, I could relax. Just really relieved.”

The driver McLaren let go

Ugochukwu was born in New York in April 2007 and signed by McLaren’s young driver programme in 2021, at thirteen. The junior record is good: Euro 4 champion with Prema in 2023, runner-up in Italian F4 the same year, winner of the Macau Grand Prix in 2024. Then a first F3 season with Prema in 2025 that returned sixteenth in the standings and no wins, and in November McLaren cut him loose along with Martinius Stenshorne and Brando Badoer.

He spent the winter in New Zealand, won the Formula Regional Oceania title with four wins, came back to F3 with Campos, and tested an Alpine at Monza in June. “We were super clinical, no mistakes made the whole weekend,” he said on Sunday, “and we just delivered when we had to.” That is a fair description of the whole year. Two wins, and a qualifying record that put him in the top four on the only weekend it had to.

And the one who lost it

Slater is eighteen, British, the 2024 Italian F4 champion and the 2025 Formula Regional European champion, and in January Audi made him the first member of its new Driver Development Programme. He drove a rookie F3 season for Trident that most champions would take: eight podiums, a win in Hungary, and the championship lead into the summer break after four Feature Race podiums in a row. Then 15 points in the last five races, and one qualifying session in Madrid that his car did not survive.

He will be in Formula 2 next year with Invicta, announced on Tuesday, two days after losing the title. It is the same Trident-to-Invicta step Gabriel Bortoleto, Leonardo Fornaroli and Rafael Camara took, and all three of them arrived there as F3 champions. Slater arrives as the runner-up who led the most laps of the argument.

Our view

It is tempting to say the extra race decided the championship, and the tempting version is wrong. After Saturday the two were level on points with Ugochukwu ahead on countback. Had Madrid been an ordinary two-race weekend, the title would have gone to the same driver, by tie-break, with an asterisk the size of a season. What Sunday’s race did was remove the asterisk. Ugochukwu won it on the road, by fourteen points, having started the decider six places ahead of his rival and finished six places ahead of him.

The weekend also exposed how much of a modern F3 title is qualifying. Slater lost the championship in the twenty minutes on Friday when his car went wrong, not in the wall at Turn 19. At a circuit where nobody passed anybody, seventeenth on the grid was not a place to recover from, and he knew it before the Sprint started.

Where it leaves us

For the books: the first Formula 3 champion from the United States, a fifteen-point deficit turned into a fourteen-point margin in three races, 33 points to 4, a title decided at a circuit that was a building site a year ago in a race that did not exist in January, Campos’s second teams’ title in a row, first wins for Clerot and Taponen, the first Finnish winner in F3, and the first race of any kind at the Madring going to Theophile Nael.

Every session is on the Madrid weekend page, the final table is on the F3 standings, and the season’s results are on the results page. The official reports of Feature Race 1 and Feature Race 2 are on the series site, and Motorsport.com has the fuller interview.

McLaren spent four and a half years developing a Formula 3 champion and let him go a season early. Campos had him for one.

The title turned in twenty minutes of qualifying on Friday evening.

title.raw: Tsolov leaves Madrid with nothing, and a seven-point lead: the F2 title fight after a weekend Campos will want back
title.rendered: Tsolov leaves Madrid with nothing, and a seven-point lead: the F2 title fight after a weekend Campos will want back

content.raw:
On lap 13 of Saturday's Sprint Race, Nikola Tsolov was fifth, behind his own team-mate, and on the radio asking Campos to move Noel Leon aside so he could chase the podium. The order never came. Four laps later he brushed the wall at Turn 20, spun, and the points half of his weekend was over with the Feature Race still to come.

He came to Madrid on 177 points and he left on 177. Rafael Camara, who came on 166, left on 170, and a championship that had eleven points in it now has seven, with three rounds on the published calendar and a real question over two of them.

Saturday: the order that never came

Friday's qualifying had put Dino Beganovic on pole for Sunday from Alexander Dunne and Camara, with Tsolov fifth. For the Sprint the top ten was reversed, which put Emerson Fittipaldi and Ritomo Miyata on the front row, Leon on the second, and the two title contenders sixth and eighth.

Miyata led before the first corner and never gave it up. Behind him the race stopped almost immediately, a safety car for Kush Maini and Nicolas Varrone at Turn 7 and a separate tangle at Turn 1, and did not go green again until lap 5. By lap 13 Leon had lost third to Laurens van Hoepen and was fourth with Tsolov filling his mirrors and Camara behind them both. Tsolov had a look at Turn 1, then asked the pit wall to let him through to go after van Hoepen. Campos did not. He tried Turn 5 instead, ran out of road, and handed the place back.

On lap 17 he clipped the inside wall at Turn 20, the car came round, and the safety car came out for the second time. The official report calls it "a slight brush with the wall", which is exactly the sort of brush this circuit punishes. Miyata restarted with 1.3s in hand and won by 2.6, the first Formula 2 victory of his career and Hitech's first since the Baku Sprint a year ago. "Finally we have won a race," he said, and thanked Hitech, Morizo-san, Toyota, his family and his girlfriend. Fittipaldi took his first podium for AIX, van Hoepen was third for Trident, and Leon's fourth gave Campos five points where Tsolov's had given them none. Camara's sixth was worth three. Eleven became eight.

Sunday: a penalty, and it did not matter

Beganovic won the Feature Race from pole and led every lap, the first F2 win of his career, "a great weekend, very good pace" and "the bounce back from Monza" in his words, seven seconds clear of Dunne with Miyata third for a second podium of the weekend. How the rest of it fell out is a story about two safety cars and who had pitted before them.

The first came on lap 6, when Maini went into the wall at Turn 18 after contact with Cian Shields. Most of the midfield took its stop in the laps that followed, Camara among them, onto hards, and came out behind Mari Boya, who had stopped early onto softs and was flying. Tsolov, who had started fifth on the hard tyre, stopped on lap 14 for softs and came out ahead of Camara. For about four laps the championship leader was where he needed to be.

Then, on lap 18, Camara and Oliver Goethe touched on the exit of Turns 1 and 2 and Goethe went into the barrier. Second safety car. The six cars that had not yet stopped, Beganovic, Dunne, Miyata, Fittipaldi, Joshua Durksen and Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak, all pitted for next to nothing and came out as the top six, and the drivers who had stopped under green were left racing for seventh. The stewards gave Camara ten seconds for the contact.

Here is the odd part. The penalty cost him one place, ninth to tenth, one point instead of two. Tsolov, whose soft tyres had eighteen laps on them by the end, was passed by car after car on the penultimate lap and finished eighteenth. Camara left with four points for the weekend. Tsolov left with none, and the gap is seven.

The table

Tsolov leads on 177. Camara is second on 170, Gabriele Mini third on 153 after a seventh place he salvaged despite missing the cheap stop, Dunne fourth on 139 after his second place, and Leon fifth on 119. Beganovic's win moves him to 106. Four drivers are within 38 points of the lead, and the leader has now had the weekend he was afraid of.

Inthraphuvasak deserves a line of his own. His car caught fire against the wall at Turn 18 in Friday practice, he took no part in qualifying, and he finished sixth on Sunday.

Our view

Tsolov's crash was his own, and nobody at Campos put him in the wall. But the situation he was in when it happened was theirs. A team with its two cars fourth and fifth on the road has a teams' championship to think about and every reason not to swap them, and a team with its title leader eleven points clear and his rival two places behind has every reason to. Campos chose the first logic on Saturday and it cost them the second. Leon's five points went into the teams' table; Tsolov's would have gone into the only fight that will be remembered.

Camara, for his part, got away with one. Putting another car into the barrier in the middle of a title fight and losing a single point for it is the sort of arithmetic that only works because the safety car he caused wrecked everyone else's afternoon more than his own. He will not get that twice.

Where it goes now

Baku is next, on the last weekend of September. After that the published calendar says Qatar at the end of November and Abu Dhabi in the first week of December, and whether either happens is Formula 1's decision rather than Formula 2's. Stefano Domenicali said in Madrid that the schedule holds as published, and that the season would finish in Europe if the last two rounds could not run; the reporting points at Imola, and the decision was due this week. F2 goes where F1 goes. A seven-point lead with three rounds left is one thing. With one, it is a different championship, and the driver who just scored nothing for a weekend would rather it stayed at three.

Where it leaves us

For the books: a leader who arrived on 177 and left on 177, a team order asked for and not given, a wall at Turn 20, an eighteenth place on Sunday, a ten-second penalty that cost one point, first wins for Miyata and Beganovic, a first podium for Emerson Fittipaldi, Hitech's first victory in a year, and a gap of seven with Baku next.

Both races are on the Madrid weekend page, the table is on the F2 standings, and the season so far is on the results page. The official reports of the Sprint and the Feature Race are on the series site.

Tsolov has a seven-point lead and a fortnight to think about how he spent four of the eleven he arrived with. Baku next.

title.raw: Why is the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on a Saturday this year?
title.rendered: Why is the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on a Saturday this year?

content.raw:
Formula 1 races on Sunday. It has for so long that the word barely needs saying in a race preview. This weekend it does not apply: the Azerbaijan Grand Prix is run on Saturday 26 September, at 15:00 in Baku. Qualifying was brought forward too, run today rather than tomorrow. Practice went with it, both Thursday sessions and Friday's third one, all a full day ahead of where an Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend normally sits.

Azerbaijan's Remembrance day

The reason is not a design quirk of the calendar or a broadcaster's request. It is in the FIA's own release from 30 June 2025, titled plainly a calendar update: "following a request from the Azerbaijan promoter and relevant government stakeholders, FIA and Formula 1 have agreed to move the 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix from Sunday 27th September to Saturday 26th to accommodate a national day." That is the whole of the FIA's stated reason. The release does not name the day itself, and it notes the change was still pending sign-off from the World Motor Sport Council when it was announced. This weekend's schedule is the confirmation that it went through.

What that day is has to be reported rather than quoted from F1 or the FIA, since neither has said so directly. ESPN and several other outlets identify 27 September as Azerbaijan's Remembrance Day, a day of mourning for the country's dead from the 44-day war with Armenia and Artsakh over Nagorno-Karabakh in the autumn of 2020, sometimes called the Patriotic War. Azerbaijan's president signed the order establishing the day that December, in the weeks after the ceasefire. Racing through it was evidently not something the promoter wanted to ask of the country, so the whole weekend moved a day earlier instead of just the race.

Other non-Sunday Races

Baku is not the only Saturday race on this year's calendar, but it is a different kind of one. Las Vegas has run on a Saturday every year since it joined the calendar in 2023, and does so again in November: a night race built around road closures and the city's own entertainment programme around it, according to GRANDE PRÊMIO, not a one-off accommodation. Its late start also means the race lands in the small hours of Sunday morning for European viewers anyway. Baku, run at 15:00 local on a Saturday afternoon, does not have that excuse or that logic.

The closest precedent is more recent than most of Formula 1's history: 2024, when the season opened with back-to-back Saturday races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia's race went to Saturday to keep it clear of the start of Ramadan, expected on 10 March that year. Bahrain, racing the week before, then moved to Saturday as well, partly because of Formula 1's own rule on the minimum gap between events once Saudi Arabia shifted, and partly because of the freight run between the two venues. Between them, ESPN reported, they made Bahrain the first world championship season-opener held on a Saturday since the 1982 South African Grand Prix.

Go back further and Saturday racing was not even unusual. For most of the 1950s, 60s and 70s a Saturday race was the default rather than the exception: the British Grand Prix ran on Saturdays from 1950 (the very first world championship race of all, at Silverstone) through 1975, and again in 1977, 1979, 1981 and 1983, 30 Saturdays in all. South Africa's Grand Prix did much the same across most of 1962 to 1985, 18 times. A handful of others moved for their own specific reasons: the 1978 Swedish Grand Prix went to Saturday to avoid clashing with the football World Cup, and the two Formula 1 races run in the car park of Caesars Palace in Las Vegas, in 1981 and 1982, were Saturday afternoon affairs, nothing like the night show the desert gets now. The 1985 South African Grand Prix at Kyalami, The Race noted, left Nigel Mansell as the last driver to win a full points race on anything other than a Sunday, until Las Vegas came along decades later.

Counting all of it precisely depends on what gets counted. GRANDE PRÊMIO put the tally at 63 Saturday world championship races once this weekend's is added, but that figure folds in two Indianapolis 500s, in 1953 and 1959, which counted toward the drivers' championship at the time without being run to Formula 1's own rules. Strip those out and it is 61 conventional Grands Prix on a Saturday, 60 before Baku joined them.

None of those older races, or Bahrain and Saudi Arabia's in 2024, or Las Vegas's by design, moved for the reason Baku has this year. Weather, a religious calendar, a broadcast market, a circuit's own build, a football tournament: Formula 1 has rearranged itself around all of them before. A government and a promoter asking for a Sunday back so their country is not racing through a day of mourning is its own category, and a rarer one. Whether it happens again is not something either side has said.

Every session from here is on the Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend page; qualifying, run earlier today, is on the qualifying page, and Saturday's race will be on the race page once the lights go out.

title.raw: Russell's Thursday lap nobody beat: Baku's three practice sessions by the numbers
title.rendered: Russell’s Thursday lap nobody beat: Baku’s three practice sessions by the numbers

content.raw:
Three practice sessions ran at Baku before qualifying this afternoon, and the single fastest lap of the lot was set first, not last. George Russell put in 1:43.347 on Thursday afternoon, in second practice, and it was still standing at the end of Friday morning's session. Nobody in first practice or third practice got near it. Here is what the fastest laps and the long runs from all three sessions actually show, read straight from OpenF1's timing data through Paddock's own practice numbers.

Russell led Thursday

Thursday morning set the baseline. Russell led first practice on a 1:45.387, four tenths clear of Max Verstappen in second (1:45.787) and Charles Leclerc in third (1:45.791), with Lewis Hamilton fourth (1:45.824) to make it a top four covered by 0.437 seconds. Kimi Antonelli was fifth, 0.878 seconds back. At the other end, Valtteri Bottas was slowest of the twenty two cars that set a time, on 1:49.315.

Second practice, that same Thursday afternoon, was quicker across the board, Russell's own benchmark dropping by just over two seconds from morning to afternoon. Mercedes had the top two times: Russell's 1:43.347 from Antonelli's 1:43.899, half a second back. Verstappen was closest of the rest in third, 0.827 seconds off Russell, with Leclerc fourth (1:44.473, +1.126) and Hamilton fifth (1:44.665, +1.318). Lando Norris led the McLarens in sixth, 1.484 seconds off Russell's pace, with Pierre Gasly, Oscar Piastri and Isack Hadjar covered by 0.025 seconds directly behind him.

Verstappen topped FP3

Friday morning's third practice was the tightest session of the weekend at the front, but it still did not produce a lap to match Thursday's. Qualifying this afternoon

None of the free practice results decide Saturday since they revealed nothing: Thursday brought the fastest lap, Friday tightened the single-lap pace but not reaching Russell's 43.3 FP2 and we are left wondering why all long runs were completed on softs. title.raw: Ninety-three minutes late and worth the wait: Verstappen's first win of 2026, Russell's car stopped, and a lead of 84
title.rendered: Ninety-three minutes late and worth the wait: Verstappen’s first win of 2026, Russell’s car stopped, and a lead of 84

content.raw:
The Bahrain Grand Prix was supposed to happen in April. It happened on the first Sunday of October, in Malaysia, 93 minutes after its scheduled start, and it was worth the wait. Max Verstappen won it from pole with the fastest lap thrown in, his first victory of 2026 and his 72nd in all; Kimi Antonelli was second and left with a championship lead of 84 points; George Russell, who had been third with six laps to go, was given a ride by a marshal.

Verstappen beat Antonelli by 2.307s, with Lewis Hamilton third from seventeenth place at one stage, Charles Leclerc fourth and Isack Hadjar fifth. The full classification is on the race page.

The result

Ninety-three minutes

The rain arrived with the cars on their way to the grid. Race Control held the start for 40 minutes, sent the field out behind the Safety Car when the water had drained enough, and then watched the formation laps fall apart: Verstappen reported over the radio that he could not accelerate, Hamilton's Ferrari ground to a halt on the start and finish straight before it would go again, and more cars were caught. The red flag came out, the cars returned to the pit lane, and the FIA sent every team a software update that removed the energy limit in the affected sectors while the clock ran another 53 minutes; the second start used the original grid order. The FIA's explanation, as reported afterwards, was "an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit's sector configuration" that had cost a number of cars their power.

When the race finally started, two laps behind the Safety Car and then a standing start at the beginning of lap 3, 13 of the 22 cars had left the pits on slicks and nine on intermediates, and five of the slick runners changed their minds behind the Safety Car before the standing start. The nine were right. Lando Norris put it plainly afterwards: "The initial gamble to start on the medium tyres didn't work out." Valtteri Bottas, who had chosen softs, lost the Cadillac at Turn 13 after seven laps and brought out the first Safety Car on lap 9: "It was always going to be a risk starting on the slicks with the soft tyre compound and today, it didn't quite pay off."

How Verstappen took it back

He had lost it first. Antonelli and Russell, both on intermediates, swept past the Red Bull into Turn 1 and ran one-two for Mercedes, with Verstappen holding off Liam Lawson for third. He passed Russell around the outside of Turn 4 on lap 6, pitted for slicks with the rest of the intermediate runners under the Safety Car, and on lap 13, at the restart, went around the outside of Antonelli into Turn 1 and completed the move at Turn 2. Russell took second from his team-mate at Turn 5 the same lap; Antonelli, who had told his engineer he had "more pace", took it back at Turn 4 on lap 21.

From there Verstappen built a lead of more than ten seconds and would have won by that much but for the second neutralisation. Alexander Albon's Williams stopped with a gearbox failure, the virtual safety car became a full one while the car was recovered, and the field closed up for a restart with the win still to be settled. Verstappen settled it. "What an incredible result!" he said. "The race was not made easy for us with all the decisions we had to make and then the Safety Car at the end on top of everything." The win is the first for Red Bull as an engine maker, in the first season of Red Bull Ford Powertrains; Laurent Mekies called it "another milestone moment in the history of this Team", and Verstappen said it was "very emotional to win with our own engine". It is also the first Ford-powered Grand Prix win since Brazil 2003.

Six laps from a double podium

Mercedes had the better of the first half. Russell's stop came earlier than he wanted, "Why have we pulled the trigger so early?", and Antonelli's soon after, but the two of them were still second and third behind the Safety Car with the podium in hand. Then, on lap 49, Russell's car ground to a halt on the start and finish straight, with what Mercedes called an apparent power unit failure. "That was another tough and disappointing day for me amongst several we have had this season," he said. "It is pure bad luck, but it still hurts." Toto Wolff: "This has been our worst weekend of the season. It hurts, and I feel incredibly sorry for George and everyone in the team."

Antonelli's reading was narrower and probably right: "Overall, given our struggles this weekend, I think P2 was the maximum we could have achieved today." Second was worth 18 points, and with Russell on none the gap between them went from 66 to 84.

Our view: the stoppage cost Russell fifteen points and the championship cost him more than that some time ago. He has had the worse luck of the two, by his own account and his team's, but 84 points with seven rounds left is not a gap that luck explains on its own. What Sunday did settle is that the title is now Antonelli's to lose.

Hamilton's afternoon

Hamilton started on the front row on soft slicks, had no grip, and was down in seventeenth place early on. Ferrari wanted him in for intermediates, as Leclerc had been; after a back-and-forth with the pit wall he stayed out on the softs, and was fifth within ten laps of the lap 13 restart. He stopped once the track had dried, passed Hadjar for third after the final restart, and finished 4.9s behind the winner at a circuit where he has five poles. "Sepang is always a great track to race on," he said, "but today is definitely one of the most memorable." Fred Vasseur: "Overall our result is good, especially considering where we were at the end of the first lap."

Leclerc's race ran the other way and arrived at the same place. "A lot of things went wrong in the first part, and everything that could have gone right did in the second part, so I would say P4 is a good result today all things considered." He took fourth from Hadjar a lap after Hamilton had taken third; Hadjar, who had started eighth after a five-place penalty for his seventh engine, said he "didn't have the power after the restart at the end for two laps".

The rest of it

Oscar Piastri was sixth for McLaren and Norris ninth: the gravel at Turn 1 under the Safety Car dropped him to eleventh, he recovered two places, and the stewards gave him a reprimand for driving erratically, his first of the season. Lawson's seventh and Arvid Lindblad's tenth, from 22nd on the grid after a 30-place penalty for his power unit changes, gave Racing Bulls two scores; Fernando Alonso was eighth for Aston Martin, "a good result for us" after his best qualifying of the year.

Carlos Sainz had climbed to sixth before Gabriel Bortoleto went down the inside of him at Turn 2 on the lap 13 restart and spun him. The stewards gave Bortoleto ten seconds and no benefit of the doubt: he "did not have his front axle alongside" the Williams' mirror before the apex, "was not in full control of the overtaking manoeuvre and was wholly to blame", and because the circumstances normally associated with a first-lap or restart incident were not present, the leniency usually shown at a restart did not apply. Bortoleto did not argue: "First of all, I want to apologise to Carlos. I made contact with him at the restart." Audi were also fined 30,000 euros, 20,000 of them suspended, for an unsafe act during Nico Hulkenberg's pit stop. Albon's driving in the pit entry road was investigated and left alone.

What it did to the championship

[[standings series=f1]]

Antonelli leaves Malaysia on 320. Russell is second on 236, Hamilton third on 214, Leclerc fourth on 191, and Norris and Verstappen are level on 188, Norris ahead on his two wins to Verstappen's one. Antonelli has eight of the sixteen wins.

Seven races remain and one sprint, at Singapore this coming weekend, which makes 183 points still on the table. He cannot clinch the title in Singapore whatever happens. Austin, on 25 October, is the earliest: he would need to leave Texas 126 or more clear of Russell, which means outscoring him by 42 across the next two rounds, and 126 clear of Hamilton as well.

The FIA's points sheet still carries the footnote it has carried for three races: subject to Audi's notice of intention to appeal against a stewards' decision from the Italian Grand Prix. That table is still not quite final.

Where it leaves us

[[chart series=f1]]

For the books: the first Formula 1 weekend in Malaysia since 2017, run under Bahrain's name after the April date was lost and the move to Sepang was announced in July; a start delayed 93 minutes; Verstappen's 49th pole, 72nd win and the fastest lap, 1:38.220 on the last lap; the first win for Red Bull Ford Powertrains and for a Ford engine since 2003; Russell's car stopped six laps from a podium; a lead of 84.

The full classification is on the race page, Saturday is on the qualifying page, the whole weekend is on the Bahrain Grand Prix hub, and the running totals are on the standings page.

Singapore next, under the lights on 11 October, with the last sprint of the season on the Saturday.

title.raw: Verstappen takes his first pole of 2026 at Sepang, three tenths clear of Hamilton, with Mercedes fourth and eighth
title.rendered: Verstappen takes his first pole of 2026 at Sepang, three tenths clear of Hamilton, with Mercedes fourth and eighth

content.raw:
Formula 1 had not qualified in Malaysia since 2017, and when it did again Max Verstappen treated Sepang as if nobody had been away. He was fastest in Q1, fastest in Q2 and fastest twice in Q3, and his final lap of 1:35.130 gave him his first pole position of 2026, the 49th of his career and his first since the Abu Dhabi finale last December. Lewis Hamilton, who has five poles of his own at this circuit, was 0.298s behind for Ferrari. The championship leader qualified fourth and the man chasing him eighth.

The lap

Verstappen's first run in Q3 was a 1:35.250, three tenths clear of his team-mate Isack Hadjar, and it would have been enough. He went out again anyway, could not improve through the first two sectors, and then found enough in the last one to go 0.120s quicker still. "It's fantastic," he said. "We've been trying many Grands Prix to get pole, sometimes a bit closer than others, but to finally get it from where we started the season, it's pretty incredible." The pole was also the first for Red Bull as a complete manufacturer, in the sixteenth Grand Prix of its own power unit's first season, which Laurent Mekies called "a special moment".

Hamilton was second, 0.298s away. "First of all, a huge thank you to everyone in the team," he said, and talked about tyre management for Sunday, as everyone did. Hadjar's 1:35.558 was good for third and worth eighth: a five-place penalty for his seventh engine of the season was already waiting for him. "Mixed feelings for me today," he said. "Obviously, we can be very happy with P1 and P3."

Mercedes' Saturday

Kimi Antonelli had been strong in the final practice session and said it was a shame to have dropped back from there. A Q2 lap was deleted for track limits, which cost him a set of tyres and left him one set of softs for Q3, and his 1:35.631 was fourth, promoted to third on the grid by Hadjar's penalty. He blamed the place rather than the car: "It is a unique circuit here with a very aggressive tarmac and in incredibly hot conditions; that makes it difficult to deliver the same performance consistently."

George Russell was eighth, seven tenths off pole, and did not dress it up. "We've struggled today and that is reflected by what was our toughest Saturday of the year." Toto Wolff used the same words and added that Friday's long runs had not been the team's strongest either, with the degradation seen in practice pointing to more than one stop. For the Mercedes of the championship leader, a Saturday with its cars fourth and eighth was the real story of the session.

The rest of the top ten

Charles Leclerc was fifth, 0.035s behind Antonelli, and unhappy with a set-up he called too aggressive after the rear slid from the second sector onwards. "P4 is not a bad place to start from. At the same time, it wasn't a great qualifying." Lando Norris was sixth and Oscar Piastri seventh for McLaren, the two of them five thousandths apart; Norris was "pretty satisfied" with a lap he felt he had put together, on a weekend when the car lacked straight-line speed and, in his words, the Red Bulls were in a class of their own. Pierre Gasly was ninth. Gabriel Bortoleto was tenth, his first Q3 since Zandvoort, after a weekend he said felt easy in the car: "I'm very happy, I think it was a mega lap."

Bortoleto's lap put Liam Lawson out of the top ten by 0.209s. Fernando Alonso was twelfth, a second and a half from the front in Q2, "our best Qualifying so far this season" in a car that lacks straight-line performance but, he said, suits this track better; Carlos Sainz was thirteenth and Lance Stroll fourteenth, his most competitive result of the year. Franco Colapinto set no time in Q2 at all, with his grid penalties already known: five places for the collision in Baku and ten for a new engine, 21st on the grid. Arvid Lindblad was sixteenth on the sheet and 22nd on the grid, after power unit changes that the stewards priced at ten places each, 30 in all.

Nico Hulkenberg missed Q2 by 0.087s. Formula 1 had not qualified in Malaysia since 2017, and when it did again Max Verstappen treated Sepang as if nobody had been away. He was fastest in Q1, fastest in Q2 and fastest twice in Q3, and his final lap of 1:35.130 gave him his first pole position of 2026, the 49th of his career and his first since the Abu Dhabi finale last December. Lewis Hamilton, who has five poles of his own at this circuit, was 0.298s behind for Ferrari. The championship leader qualified fourth and the man chasing him eighth.

The lap

Verstappen’s first run in Q3 was a 1:35.250, three tenths clear of his team-mate Isack Hadjar, and it would have been enough. He went out again anyway, could not improve through the first two sectors, and then found enough in the last one to go 0.120s quicker still. “It’s fantastic,” he said. “We’ve been trying many Grands Prix to get pole, sometimes a bit closer than others, but to finally get it from where we started the season, it’s pretty incredible.” The pole was also the first for Red Bull as a complete manufacturer, in the sixteenth Grand Prix of its own power unit’s first season, which Laurent Mekies called “a special moment”.

Hamilton was second, 0.298s away. “First of all, a huge thank you to everyone in the team,” he said, and talked about tyre management for Sunday, as everyone did. Hadjar’s 1:35.558 was good for third and worth eighth: a five-place penalty for his seventh engine of the season was already waiting for him. “Mixed feelings for me today,” he said. “Obviously, we can be very happy with P1 and P3.”

Kimi Antonelli had been strong in the final practice session and said it was a shame to have dropped back from there. He blamed the place rather than the car: “It is a unique circuit here with a very aggressive tarmac and in incredibly hot conditions; that makes it difficult to deliver the same performance consistently.”

For the Mercedes of the championship leader, a Saturday with its cars fourth and eighth was the real story of the session.

title.raw: Verstappen comes for the one win Singapore has never given him
title.rendered: Verstappen comes for the one win Singapore has never given him

content.raw:
Max Verstappen's dominance is beyond dispute: four championships, 72 wins, 49 pole positions and 135 podiums. There are only six tracks where the Dutchman has never won, and he has raced more than twice at only two of them. One is the Sochi Autodrom in Russia (banned since 2021). The other, as you may have guessed, is the Marina Bay Street Circuit. Verstappen has raced the Singapore Grand Prix every year since 2015. This weekend marks his tenth visit and his 250th Grand Prix, and he arrives as the winner of the last race.

That last part is new for 2026. Verstappen won the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia from pole on Sunday, his first win of the year and, in team principal Laurent Mekies' words, "this first victory with a homegrown engine" for Red Bull Racing. Verstappen was clearly the fastest driver in Sepang, helped by a Mercedes upgrade that cost them a lot of time. Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said: "You're expecting three tenths to kick in and it looks like [we've gone] three or four or five tenths backwards," adding: "It's the first time we miss out on the top three, and by quite a chunk. So it's odd, but I guess we will find a solution."

Second, second, second

Verstappen's Singapore record reads like a list of near misses. Second in 2018 behind Lewis Hamilton. Third in 2019. Second in 2024 behind Lando Norris, and second again last year behind George Russell. He has started from the front row four times and never from pole.

The other years were worse. In 2017 he lined up second and was out at the first corner, caught in a collision with both Ferraris. In 2023, the season Red Bull won 21 of 22 races, Singapore was the one they lost; he qualified 11th and finished fifth.

A street circuit he likes but can't win at

None of that has put him off the place. "I enjoy this track as a street circuit, and it has a lot of corners and is quite bumpy," he said this week. "Singapore is a race that I haven't won before, so it does feel like unfinished business at this track."

Jeddah, another street circuit raced under lights, has been a different story. In five visits from 2021 to 2025 he finished second, first, second, first and second, including second from 15th on the grid in 2023. But Jeddah is fast and flowing. Marina Bay is slow, walled and bumpy: of all the tracks F1 races on, only Monaco has a lower average speed.

Verstappen is careful not to read too much into Sepang. "I think the win was quite track specific so we will need to see how we go heading into this week," he said.

Mercedes have left a door open

Mercedes have won 11 of the 16 races this year and lead the championship through Kimi Antonelli, on 320 points, 84 clear of Russell. They arrive with problems of their own. Russell takes a new power unit and starts Sunday's race from the back of the grid, although the penalty does not touch Saturday's Sprint.

Mercedes have stated that they will run two different cars all weekend, their latest aerodynamic package against the previous one, after the dreadful update in Malaysia. It is still to be decided who will get the worse of the two cars, but we at Paddock expect it will be Russell, whose weekend is already compromised.

The other Red Bull

Isack Hadjar has scored in each of his last nine starts, a run that spans the three races he missed with a fractured wrist. He was blunt about the conditions: "The conditions are always brutal here, but I have experience from last year and even from last week in Malaysia. It's not something I'm worried about."

His read of the weekend matches his team's: "If we can take the performance from Baku and the learnings from Malaysia, we're in for a positive weekend."

Our view

Red Bull will not claim more than they know. Asked whether the car is now good enough to fight for the win at every circuit, Mekies answered: "Impossible to say."

Singapore is the first proper answer. If the Sepang form belonged to Sepang, Verstappen's tenth attempt will look like the other nine. If it belongs to the car, the one race he has never won has rarely looked more open, with one Mercedes starting at the back and the team that has won 11 of 16 races still working out which of its two cars is the quick one.

Session times and the full entry are on the weekend page, and the standings update as the results land.

title.raw: The corner is gone, but the men behind Crashgate are back
title.rendered: The corner is gone, but the men behind Crashgate are back

content.raw:
On lap 14 of the first Singapore Grand Prix, in 2008, Nelson Piquet Jr put his Renault into the wall at Turn 17. He did it on purpose. Two laps earlier his teammate Fernando Alonso had made the first pit stop of the race, and the safety car that followed turned that early stop into a win from 15th on the grid.

Formula 1 returns to Marina Bay this weekend with the man who ran that Renault team, Flavio Briatore, running it again. It races today as Alpine, from the same factory in Enstone. Pat Symonds, who participated in the planning and helped engineer the logistics, later admitting to a "misguided devotion" to the team, is now the executive engineering consultant for the Cadillac Formula One Team.

A quick car, a lost Saturday

Renault arrived in Singapore without a win since 2006; their prized driver, Fernando Alonso, had not stood on a podium all season. Then, out of nowhere, their car was quick: Alonso was fastest in second practice on Friday and again in final practice on Saturday.

Qualifying, however, crushed their only hope of a win. A fuel problem stopped Alonso's car early in Q2, before he could set a time, forcing him to start from 15th. "Since Friday we knew that the car was very competitive," Briatore said after the race, "and we were very disappointed at the end of qualifying."

A strategy that made no sense, until the rule

From the back of the grid, on a track where nobody could pass, the usual plan was a heavy car: run long while the cars ahead stopped, and gain places in the pits. Renault did the opposite. They sent Alonso out on a very short first stint, which meant a light car and an early stop that would drop him behind almost everyone. Afterwards, Alonso put it down to worries about the brakes.

What made the outrageous strategy work was a rule that had only been in effect for the past two seasons. The pit lane closed when the safety car came out and stayed closed until the whole field had queued up behind it, penalising any driver who pitted in the meantime. A safety car therefore wiped out every gap and sent the leaders into the pits together, and a driver who had pitted just before it would jump almost the whole field.

The scandal

Alonso pitted on lap 12, the first driver to stop, and rejoined at the back. Two laps later, it happened: Piquet floored the throttle and put his R28 into the wall. When the pit lane opened, nearly everyone came in at once.

Alonso came out of the whole shuffle in fifth position, behind four cars that had yet to make their stops or serve their penalties. By lap 34 he led, and he won by 2.957 seconds from Nico Rosberg, with Lewis Hamilton third.

Massa's fuel hose

Felipe Massa had led from pole. In the rush of stops, Ferrari released him with the fuel hose still attached, and he dragged it the length of the pit lane before his mechanics could pull it off. He rejoined last, collected a drive-through penalty for the unsafe release and finished 13th, with no points.

None of that was Renault's doing, but it shaped the title race: Hamilton arrived in Singapore one point ahead of Massa and left seven points clear.

Why so clever

At the time it was an accident: Piquet said he had "lost the rear" of his car, and Renault praised Alonso's "brilliant tactical drive".

Piquet had been desperate to keep his seat: Briatore, he said, had refused to tell him whether his contract would be renewed. Ten months after the race, as Renault dropped him, he gave a statement to the FIA setting out how that safety car was arranged. After a meeting with Briatore and Symonds, he said, Symonds took him aside and, with a map, pointed him to the exact corner where he should crash. "This corner was selected because the specific location of the track did not have any cranes," Piquet said, "nor did it have any side entrances to the track". A car stranded there would need the safety car. He was told the lap as well, and he made sure of it: "I asked my team several times via the radio to confirm the lap number, which I would not normally do."

The telemetry backed him up, and Symonds admitted the idea had been discussed, though in his account "it was [Piquet] who first suggested" it. Briatore denied there had been any plan.

The verdict, and the reversal

On 21 September 2009, the FIA's World Motor Sport Council handed down its verdict. Renault were disqualified from the championship, a sentence suspended for two years, while Briatore was banned indefinitely and Symonds for five years. Piquet escaped punishment altogether, having been promised immunity in exchange for his evidence, and Alonso was cleared of any involvement. The result stood, and it still does.

The bans, on the other hand, did not last. In January 2010 a Paris court overturned both of them, and by April the FIA had settled, with Briatore and Symonds agreeing to stay out of Formula 1 until 2013.

The case that is still open

Massa lost the 2008 title to Hamilton by a single point, 98 to 97. The race was fixed, he argues, so its result should have been cancelled: take Singapore away and Hamilton finishes on 92, making Massa champion. Since 2024 he has been suing the FIA, Formula One Management and Bernie Ecclestone for £64 million, leaning on Ecclestone's 2023 interview, in which he said the race should have been cancelled "according to the rules". Ecclestone later told Reuters he did not remember giving it.

The defendants say the claim comes too late, and that Massa's and Ferrari's own errors that night cost him the title. The High Court let his conspiracy claim go to trial, which now waits on their appeal at the Supreme Court.

Our view

The sport has decided Crashgate belongs to history. The result stands, the bans were overturned, and both men the FIA punished work for teams on this grid. Only the courts are still asking what Formula 1 knew in 2008, and when.

The place where it happened has moved on too. Turn 17 sat in the section of track that ran round The Float, bypassed since 2023 while NS Square is built on the site. The cars will not pass the spot on Sunday.

Session times and the full entry are on the weekend page, and the circuit's story is on our Marina Bay page.

title.raw: Russell's Saturday, Norris's Sunday: our Singapore predictions after one hour of practice
title.rendered: Russell’s Saturday, Norris’s Sunday: our Singapore predictions after one hour of practice

content.raw:
One hour. That is all the drivers got at Marina Bay before Sprint Qualifying, and for most of it the soft tyre stayed in the blankets. When it finally came out, George Russell needed just two laps. On the older Mercedes, the one he asked to go back to after the dreadful update in Sepang, he topped FP1 with a 1:32.274, 0.198 seconds clear of Charles Leclerc and 0.273 clear of Lando Norris.

How the hour played out

Early on, everyone ran the hard tyre except Cadillac, the only team to start on mediums. Leclerc set the early benchmark, a 1:33.969 inside the first twenty minutes, before Mercedes went to the top with both cars: Kimi Antonelli on the new package with a 1:33.830, and Russell on the old one, just 0.056 seconds behind. Two very different Mercedes, almost the same lap.

Then came the long runs, a second or more slower per sector. With twenty minutes left, Nico Hülkenberg reported a gearbox problem and parked his Audi at the pit exit, bringing out the Virtual Safety Car. Fernando Alonso switched to mediums soon after and jumped to eighth with a 1:34.644.

The softs came out for the final quarter of an hour. Russell's first lap on them, a 1:32.864, was already the fastest of the day, and the tyres hung on for a second flyer: a mighty final sector of 26.002 and the 1:32.274 that nobody beat. Lewis Hamilton was on for more, with a personal best first sector of 27.249, before he bailed out. Antonelli bailed too, after a mistake of his own that left him in a cloud of smoke and dust. A lot of traffic going into the last sector caught them both.

Two more things caught our eye. Antonelli went back to the old front wing for his fast runs, according to F1 TV's Sam Collins and Sky Sport F1 in Italy, so the Mercedes split is still unanswered. And Mercedes skipped cooling vests to spend the money on the car, on a weekend with a heat hazard declared and the track at up to 52°C. Brave, or reckless.

Sprint Qualifying: Russell

Russell's best three sectors add up to 1:32.208, the quickest ideal lap of the day. The doubts: Sprint Qualifying runs at 20:30 under the floodlights, on a track Pirelli expects at 30 to 35°C, and Red Bull never put either car on the soft tyre. Neither did Antonelli. If anyone was hiding pace today, our money is on Max Verstappen.

The Sprint: Russell, Norris, Leclerc

The Sprint starts at 17:00 tomorrow, in the same daylight as today, so FP1 is the best guide we have to its 21 laps. title.raw: RedBull hides performance: Verstappen clinches Sprint Pole
title.rendered: RedBull hides performance: Verstappen clinches Sprint Pole

content.raw:
Max Verstappen took pole for Singapore's first Sprint with his only lap of SQ3, and after an evening waiting on the stewards, he keeps it. He and Lewis Hamilton were summoned at 22:15 over an alleged overtake under yellow flags in SQ1, and the stewards decided against a grid penalty: they were satisfied that Verstappen had reacted appropriately to the yellow flag, lifting off the throttle and reducing his speed.

What the stewards looked at

Four minutes into SQ1, Sergio Pérez put his Cadillac into the barrier at Turn 5 and limped on with his front wing wedged under the car, bringing out yellow flags and then a red. Under those yellows, Verstappen passed Hamilton. Hamilton reported it on the radio straight away, and Verstappen said on his own radio that he had let him back through. The stewards summoned both of them under the yellow-flag rule, Appendix H, Article 2.5.5 b) of the International Sporting Code.

Verstappen knows that rule. The last time it caught him in qualifying, in Qatar in 2021, he failed to slow for double waved yellows and the stewards took five places off him. And the last time the Singapore stewards saw him after qualifying, in 2023, they let him off with two reprimands for impeding, then admitted a week later that they should have given him a grid penalty.

It is not the first time this year the pair have talked about each other on the radio, either. In Budapest Verstappen complained that Hamilton was "again moving under braking", at Monza they blamed each other for a near-miss in practice, and in Madrid it was Hamilton telling Ferrari that "Max has got to give back the position". Singapore just added another episode.

The lap that put him there

We said that if anyone was hiding pace in FP1, our money was on Verstappen. Red Bull kept both cars off the soft tyre all afternoon, and four hours later we found out why. On his only lap of SQ3 he did a 1:31.156, 0.120 seconds clear of George Russell, our pick for Sprint pole. After nine Grands Prix here without a pole or a win, it is the first time he has topped a qualifying session of any kind at Marina Bay. He has finished second here in 2018, 2024 and 2025. For a man with 72 Grand Prix wins, Marina Bay has been the one place that keeps handing him silverware he never ordered.

A red flag, a glitch and a lock-up

The red flag left six minutes of SQ1, and then things got messy. The timing system stopped registering some lap times, which delayed SQ2, and race control made a mistake of its own: Overtake mode was not available after the restart and was then switched on for just 27 seconds. "The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars," it said afterwards. Arvid Lindblad missed SQ2 by a tenth, and Lance Stroll was reportedly on course to go through.

SQ2 nearly caught Russell out. A lock-up into Turn 13 dropped him out of the top ten before a last-ditch lap took him to fourth. Franco Colapinto missed out by 0.094 seconds to his teammate Pierre Gasly.

In SQ3, Lando Norris set the early pace and Charles Leclerc took provisional pole, then improved to 1:31.399. Leclerc was quickest through the middle sector, but Verstappen found a third of a second on him in the first. Isack Hadjar lost a 1:32.048, good enough for eighth, to track limits at Turn 19, and eighth went to an excellent Liam Lawson.

Mercedes' answer is getting louder

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff calls his drivers "two test pilots" this weekend, and after FP1 he already had a hunch: "the new car seems to be a little more tricky to drive", while "the older car is a bit more stable, grippy". Russell, on the old package, was second. Kimi Antonelli, on the upgraded car without the new front wing he gave up after FP1, was seventh, 0.573 seconds slower. If they finish the Sprint where they start, Russell takes five points out of Antonelli's 84-point lead.

What it means for the Sprint

The Sprint starts at 17:00 tomorrow, in daylight, over 21 laps. It is 198 metres from pole to the braking point for Turn 1, and 18 of the 29 Sprints so far have been won from pole. Verstappen keeps pole, and we think he wins it. Russell, with three Sprint wins already this year, is the one most likely to stop him. Leclerc and Oscar Piastri share the second row.

Session times and the full entry are on the weekend page.

title.raw: First blood to Verstappen
title.rendered: First blood to Verstappen

content.raw:
Max Verstappen finally won at Singapore, and he had to wait a lap for it. "I want to win tomorrow" he said to David Coulthard post-race "I don't see this as a win in terms of actually winning a Grand Prix". A downpour soaked the grid 15 minutes before the start, the race went off more than half an hour late on intermediates after two formation laps, and George Russell beat him off the line to lead into Turn 1. It did not last. At the final corner Russell lost control over the slippery white line and spun into the inside wall. From there Verstappen had it under control, and won by 2.6 seconds.

What the Sprint told us

Lewis Hamilton was the man of the race behind him. Up from sixth to third at the start, he had the pace to drop Charles Leclerc, whose front tyres were "destroyed" and who was losing two seconds a lap to his teammate by the end. Kimi Antonelli inched his way to fourth, which stretches his lead over Russell to 89 points.

McLaren let their drivers race, and it cost them. On the last lap Lando Norris went down the inside of Oscar Piastri, they touched, both spun, and a team that was set for nine points left with one. Pierre Gasly had a dreadful afternoon, passed by Oliver Bearman and then by Nico Hülkenberg, in a move the stewards looked at and let go.

The walls and the gremlins took the rest. Lance Stroll and Sergio Pérez took each other out at Turn 16 on the opening lap, Alexander Albon and Gabriel Bortoleto tangled at the same corner on lap 8, and Isack Hadjar parked his Red Bull with the engine braking "dying".

Qualifying: Verstappen's to lose

We think tonight is between Verstappen, Russell, Hamilton and Norris. We side with Max. He has the Sprint pole and the Sprint win, and the way he got that pole says a lot. In SQ3 on Friday, Verstappen and Hamilton did a single run each, three laps in all, while Leclerc, Russell, Antonelli and both McLarens went out twice. Verstappen's one flying lap was still the fastest of the lot. Everyone else will need the perfect lap just to have a chance.

Russell is the odd one out. He can still be quickest, but the stewards have handed him a 40-place drop for his new power unit, so he starts Sunday from the back whatever he does tonight.

Changeable conditions have upset Singapore qualifying before. In 2022 a drying track handed Leclerc pole by 0.022 seconds, and Verstappen, the champion that year, qualified eighth. The forecast shows a slight chance of drizzle tonight, which could bring out the intermediates, but we think it is unlikely, and the same goes for tomorrow's race.

Sunday: what to expect

If Verstappen takes pole, history is on his side: 11 of the 16 Singapore Grands Prix have been won from pole. Hamilton is our dark horse after that Sprint, and one more win here would equal Sebastian Vettel's record of five.

Russell starts from the back with a point to prove, and he knows these walls better than he would like. In 2023 he crashed out here on the final lap while chasing a podium. On a dry track Pirelli expects one stop, and F1 puts the chance of a safety car at 67%, which makes a climb from the back less hopeless than it sounds.

Antonelli just has to keep doing what he did today: stay out of trouble and collect. He cannot clinch the title in Singapore, but another Sunday like this would leave Russell needing something special in the last six rounds.

Session times and the full entry are on the weekend page, and the title race is on our standings page.

title.raw: Finally, a Singapore pole
title.rendered: Finally, a Singapore pole

content.raw:
Nobody could match Max Verstappen tonight, not even Verstappen himself. His first run in Q3, a 1:31.373, was perfect, and his second could not beat it: it was a quarter of a second slower and down in every sector. It is his first pole position at Marina Bay, at the tenth attempt, and the first for Red Bull here since Sebastian Vettel in 2013. Charles Leclerc was 54 thousandths behind, and Lewis Hamilton third after a disappointing last attempt.

Qualifying breakdown

The seven-time world champion was fastest in Q1 and Q2, but we suspect that was a mix of Verstappen hiding his true pace and his Red Bull's inability to downshift smoothly, which we have heard him complain about time and time again.

Then it was Kimi Antonelli, followed by the two McLarens, with Lando Norris faster than Oscar Piastri this time. No penalty came Norris's way for his mistake on the last lap of the Sprint, which ruined his and his teammate's race in a matter of a few metres.

George Russell qualified sixth but will start at the back of the grid after a 40-place grid drop for the changes Mercedes made to his power unit. Isack Hadjar will join him there after an issue-ridden Q1 that left him without a time on the board.

Pierre Gasly showed that experience pays. After a difficult weekend he qualified eighth, ahead of his true rivals, the two Racing Bulls of the team he grew up in as Toro Rosso and AlphaTauri: Liam Lawson ninth, then Arvid Lindblad.

Our predictions for tomorrow

The race is scheduled to start at 20:00 local time, although knowing Singapore's weather this weekend, that could change. Don't miss the five lights: Verstappen has shown that his only weakness is getting off the line, losing P1 instantly to Russell in the Sprint. He did the same in Sepang, falling to third behind the Mercedes drivers. That could open the field up and bring collisions or plenty of overtakes on the opening lap.

If Max holds on to P1, history will be on his side: 11 of the 16 Singapore Grands Prix have been won by the pole-sitter. Our honest opinion is that his only real enemy will be a mechanical fault, but let's not jinx it. It is his fifth front-row start here and his first pole, so it is time for him to get his revenge on Singapore.

Pirelli expects one stop on a dry track and F1 puts the chance of a safety car at 67%, so points are not out of the question even for Russell at the back. The forecast shows a slight chance of drizzle for the race, as it did for qualifying, but we think it will stay dry.

Session times and the full grid are on the weekend page, and the title race is on our standings page.
